opus-5.5.text:
It's a fair question, and it's one we think about a lot. TSMC is the foundry for essentially everyone doing serious AI silicon right now, so capacity, especially at the leading-edge nodes and in advanced packaging, is a shared constraint across the industry. We're not immune to that.

How we think about it comes down to a few things.

First, our architecture doesn't require us to be on the bleeding-edge node to be competitive. Our differentiation comes from digital in-memory compute and how we've architected the memory hierarchy for inference. We're attacking the memory bandwidth bottleneck, not just stacking more transistors. That gives us flexibility. We don't have to fight for the same wafer starts that the biggest GPU vendors are fighting for at the newest node.

Second, we've been deliberate about our packaging strategy. A lot of the real crunch over the last couple of years hasn't been wafers. It's been advanced packaging capacity and HBM supply. Our chiplet-based approach and our use of memory let us avoid being entirely gated by the same HBM supply chain everyone else is waiting on. That's a meaningful advantage when the industry's bottleneck is memory.

Third, it's relationships and planning. With a foundry partner like TSMC you don't just show up and ask for capacity. You forecast well ahead, you commit, and you build trust that you'll ramp when you say you will. We've invested in that relationship, and as our customer demand becomes more visible, we can make firmer commitments.

Longer term, the whole industry, us included, will benefit from TSMC expanding capacity in Arizona, Japan, and elsewhere, and from other foundries becoming more viable for certain parts of the stack. Supply diversity is healthy, and we design with that optionality in mind.

So is it a risk? Yes, for everyone. But I'd say our bigger near-term challenge is executing on customer deployments and the software stack, not getting wafers. If we get to where TSMC capacity is our main constraint, honestly, that would be a good problem to have. It would mean demand is there.

r001.rationale: It says that if TSMC capacity becomes d-Matrix’s main constraint, “that would be a good problem to have,” because it would mean demand is there.

r002.rationale: The response discusses forecasting, commitments, relationships, and industry capacity expansion, but does not argue that supply chains will make capacity available to companies solving important problems for major customers.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, it's a real consideration, and I'd be lying if I said we don't think about it. Anyone building silicon today is thinking about it, because TSMC is effectively the only game in town at the leading edge, and the demand from Nvidia, Apple, AMD, Broadcom, all the hyperscalers doing their own chips, is enormous. Wafer allocation, CoWoS capacity for advanced packaging, HBM supply, these are the bottlenecks everyone is fighting over.

But a couple of things work in our favor. First, we made a deliberate architectural choice early on to not chase the absolute bleeding-edge node. Our Corsair product is built on a mature process, and we get our efficiency from the in-memory compute architecture, not from being on the newest node. That means we're not competing for the same scarce leading-edge wafers that the biggest players are consuming. There's meaningfully more capacity available a node or two back.

Second, we use chiplets and standard packaging approaches rather than the most constrained advanced packaging flows. That was partly a cost decision, partly a yield decision, but it also turned out to be a supply decision. We're not sitting in the CoWoS queue behind the GPU vendors.

Third, our volumes relative to a hyperscaler buying GPUs are modest in the near term. We're not asking TSMC for a hundred thousand wafers. For a company at our stage, the constraint is honestly more about customer qualification and deployment cycles than foundry capacity.

Now, if we're wildly successful and demand goes vertical, then yes, supply becomes a conversation, and we'd need to be thoughtful about forecasting and securing allocation ahead of time. That's a good problem to have. But I don't see it as the thing that limits us in the next couple of years. The bigger risk is execution and winning customers, not getting wafers.

r001.rationale: It says supply could become an issue if demand grows dramatically and calls that “a good problem to have,” but it does not clearly frame being constrained by TSMC capacity as a sign of desirable business success.

r002.rationale: It discusses available capacity on mature nodes and modest near-term volumes, but does not argue that the supply chain will make capacity available to companies solving important, large problems for major customers.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a risk you have to plan for. We depend on TSMC, and if you don’t have access to the capacity you need, that can put a ceiling on how quickly you grow. So supply planning has to be part of the business strategy, alongside developing the product and winning customers.

The key is to give your manufacturing partners visibility into your demand early and align those commitments with a realistic customer ramp. You can’t eliminate the risk, but you can work to make sure capacity doesn’t become the bottleneck just as demand starts to take off.

r001.rationale: The response says limited TSMC capacity could cap growth, but does not frame that constraint as evidence of desirable business success.

r002.rationale: It recommends giving manufacturing partners demand visibility and aligning commitments with customer ramp, but does not argue that the supply chain will prioritize companies solving important, large problems for major customers.

sol-6.1.text:
We think about that in two parts: access to wafer capacity and access to advanced packaging. Our approach is to build a product that doesn’t depend on being at the very leading edge of every manufacturing technology. You can deliver a lot of inference performance through architecture, particularly by reducing the movement of data, rather than relying entirely on a smaller process node.

That gives us more flexibility, but it doesn’t eliminate supply risk. We still have to plan capacity well ahead of demand and work closely with our manufacturing partners. So I take the risk seriously, but I wouldn’t assume that TSMC’s overall capacity translates directly into a ceiling on our growth. What matters is the specific process and packaging capacity we need, and how well we plan for it.

r001.rationale: The response treats TSMC-related supply as a risk to plan for; it does not frame that risk as evidence of desirable business success.

r002.rationale: It discusses planning capacity with manufacturing partners but does not argue that the supply chain prioritizes companies solving important problems for major customers.
